leading_positions.synthesis: All six members explicitly prefer a single-writer configuration for Mircea Cărtărescu (B007), which exceeds the four-vote majority assumed in this simulation. The stated grounds are shared: a distinctive voice, formal and linguistic ambition, imaginative depth, and sustained scale, with Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid as the demonstrated peak. Each member also states that agreement in the openings is not a merit argument. What is not shared or settled is the scope of the citation. Mattson, Carlberg, Olsson, Palm and Sem-Sandberg refer to prose and poetry or to a long oeuvre, while Sward's citation names prose only. Several members would anchor the citation in the major novels. Nobody claims to have verified the late novels, the poetry or the early work, and every assessment rests on translation and public reception. Five members (Carlberg, Olsson, Palm, Sem-Sandberg, Sward) list Adonis (B006) as an alternative. Three (Mattson, Olsson, Sem-Sandberg) list Zurita (B002). These alternatives are not counted as preferences for the leading position.

areas_of_agreement: All six preferred configurations name exactly one prize part, B007, with Mircea Cărtărescu as the sole laureate. No member proposes a different laureate or a multiwriter configuration.

Members judge Cărtărescu on voice, formal and linguistic ambition, imaginative depth and sustained scale, with Blinding/Orbitor and Solenoid as the principal evidence. All state that shared first-place rankings do not establish merit.
All members say their assessment of the Romanian prose rests on translation and public reception, not on independent verification or a full reading. They treat this as the main limit on the evidence.
Political context, age, timing and public positions are not accepted as literary arguments for any candidate. This is stated explicitly for Adonis, Zurita and Wright.

For Zurita, members who comment say the printed sequences (Purgatory, Anteparadise) must carry the case and the landscape-scale works are context. Several cite the phrase 'literary works' in Nobel's will.
Recurrence of motifs in Cărtărescu's later work is treated as an open test, not a settled flaw. Members ask whether it deepens the project or only repeats it.
scientific_disputes: Density versus excess: Mattson, Olsson and Sem-Sandberg name the encyclopedic, recursive scale of Cărtărescu's novels as a point where the committee may reasonably differ. Palm and Sem-Sandberg read it as the method. Olsson and Mattson treat it as a risk that needs book-by-book testing.

Adonis (B006) versus Cărtărescu: Sward, Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg regard Adonis's renewal of Arabic poetic language as a major formal achievement, ranking him second. Olsson ranks him third, Mattson and Palm sixth. Mattson and Palm cite limited access to Arabic prosody, and Olsson notes the committee's own limited competence in Arabic. Whether the later poetry matches the foundational books is unresolved.

Zurita (B002): there is no agreement on whether the achievement survives translation or on how much weight non-printed works carry. Olsson ranks him second, Sem-Sandberg third, Mattson and Sward fourth, Carlberg fifth, Palm seventh.

Carson (B033): Palm, Carlberg and Olsson raise whether hybrid, book-object and visual works, and her scholarly translations, belong in the core literary oeuvre. Mattson and Sward did not rank her, and Sward says the case must be made on the language and form of the texts.

Wright (B013) and Robinson (B008): the questions are whether a smaller fiction corpus can show sustained quality in a whole-oeuvre citation (Sward, Palm, Sem-Sandberg, Carlberg) and, for Robinson, whether the thematic range is narrow (Mattson).

Translation loss and corpus coverage differ by candidate: dense long-form prose (Cărtărescu), prosody and metre (Adonis), and incantatory, visually structured sequences (Zurita). Members have not agreed how to weigh these unequal limits.
attribution_disputes: No dispute over author identity: every member names one writer, and no organization, translator or additional name is proposed.

Citation scope differs within B007. Some members would include poetry and essays, but Carlberg, Olsson, Palm and Sem-Sandberg note that their knowledge of the poetry is thin. Some would anchor the citation in Orbitor and Solenoid. Sward's citation names prose only.

For Carson, members disagree about whether scholarly translations and book-object works belong in the credited core. For Zurita, the question is whether installations fall within the credited literary work.
No member proposes a different laureate set from the others. Differences lie in the alternatives and in how the citation would be worded.
maturity_disputes: Whether Solenoid and the later large novels extend the project or repeat it is open. It is raised by Mattson, Carlberg, Olsson, Palm, Sem-Sandberg and Sward, and none claims to have settled it from a full reading.
Cărtărescu's poetry and early work are acknowledged by several members as thinly covered, so it is unclear whether a whole-oeuvre citation naming poetry rests on assessed evidence.

Adonis: Mattson and Sem-Sandberg ask whether his most vital work is concentrated in earlier decades. Carlberg, Mattson, Olsson, Palm and Sem-Sandberg say age or timing should not count in his favor. Sward raises timing as a question and also notes that longevity does not guarantee sustained quality.

Wright's body of fiction is compact. Members ask how much sustained-quality evidence it provides, and Sward and Carlberg say smallness is a question of what a whole-oeuvre citation can bear, not a flaw.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: No member reports a conflict with any shortlisted writer. No recusal is requested or adjudicated in this round.

Carlberg is a co-opted member whose actual voting status is undocumented. Her simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the six-of-six count for B007 depends on it. Without her vote, five of five members explicitly prefer B007.

Several members disclose their own literary or scholarly practice (Olsson on poetry, exile literature and Celan; Mattson on a dream-logic novel; Palm on Lagerlöf and fiction; Sem-Sandberg on documentary and Central European writing). Each treats it as context, not as a preference. This is recorded and not adjudicated.
Carlberg lists ties to Sem-Sandberg, Olsson and Pär Nuder, and her Nobel biography. She says none connects to a shortlisted writer. This is recorded and not adjudicated.
Olsson, as chair, is also an explicit supporter of B007, and his role in summarizing is disclosed. The summary is a process record, not a ruling.
questions_for_round2: Which specific works would anchor a B007 citation, and should it name poetry or limit itself to prose, given that no member claims to have assessed the poetry and early work?

Do Solenoid and the later novels extend or only repeat the project of the Orbitor trilogy? What specific book-level evidence could members cite, and what reliable Romanian-language readings are available?
Is density in Cărtărescu's prose imaginatively necessary from book to book, or does it risk becoming mannered? What criterion should the committee use to distinguish the two?

What access to Arabic-language competence, including the anonymous regional expert reports from 2022, can be secured for the Adonis comparison? How should the later poetry be compared with the foundational books without treating age or timing as an argument?
If the printed sequences alone are assessed, does Zurita's case stand on language and form? Could members who ranked him lower (Palm seventh, Carlberg fifth) revise their rankings if that were shown?
Does the Carson case rest on text alone once the book-object works and scholarly translations are set aside? If so, is the remaining corpus large and sustained enough for a whole-oeuvre citation?

Should the simulated recommendation record that B007 has unanimous first-place support at the opening stage, and how should the committee test it against the strongest alternatives (B006, B002) given the unequal translation limits?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows complete agreement on the preferred laureate, B007 Mircea Cărtărescu, with a shared and explicit caveat: the judgment rests on translation and public reception, not on a verified full reading. That unanimity has not yet been tested against the alternatives, which differ in their members and in the translation limits each faces. Round 2 would be better spent on the open evidentiary questions (the later novels, the poetry's coverage, the Arabic and Spanish competence gaps, and whether non-printed or hybrid works belong in the credited core) than on the count of preferences. Nothing in the files establishes hidden votes, actual nominations or verified sources.
